sourceNote: NBER business cycle dates, BLS unemployment rates, and Dow Jones / S&P 500 price history. Figures are rounded and market recovery times are approximate, in nominal terms.

recessions.name: The Great Depression
recessions.story: Nine thousand banks failed and took deposits down with them — there was no FDIC. The Dow lost 89% and did not see its 1929 high again until 1954.

recessions.name: The 1937 Relapse
recessions.story: The double dip nobody remembers. Spending cuts and tightening hit an economy still on crutches, and stocks were cut in half in twelve months.

recessions.name: The Oil Shock
recessions.story: The OPEC embargo quadrupled oil prices while inflation ran hot — stagflation. Stocks fell by half and took the rest of the decade to climb back.

recessions.name: The Volcker Double-Dip
recessions.story: The Fed pushed rates near 20% to kill inflation and triggered two recessions back to back. Brutal for jobs and borrowers — but the market snapped back fast once rates fell.

recessions.name: The Early '90s Recession
recessions.story: An oil price spike after the invasion of Kuwait, a credit crunch, and the S&L cleanup. Short and shallow — but the jobless recovery dragged on for years.

recessions.name: The Dot-Com Bust
recessions.story: GDP barely dipped, but the market carnage was real: the S&P halved and the Nasdaq lost 78%. Concentrated pain for tech workers and anyone holding growth stocks.

recessions.name: The Great Recession
recessions.story: A housing collapse became a global credit freeze. Nearly nine million jobs disappeared, home prices fell by a third, and the median spell of unemployment stretched past six months.

recessions.name: The COVID Crash
recessions.story: The fastest crash and fastest recovery on record. Twenty-two million jobs vanished in two months — a reminder that the shock you plan for is rarely the one you get.
